title: Dracula
synopsis: London by mail coach. A solicitor's clerk goes to Transylvania for a real estate sale. The count, you'll find, casts no reflection.

nodes.text: The coach driver takes your money at the Borgo Pass without meeting your eyes, and is gone before the dust settles. Then the calèche comes for you: black horses, a driver who does not speak, a hand cold enough to feel through your glove. Wolves close on the road and he lifts one arm, and they part for him like water.

choices.consequence: You keep your voice level and your hands still. The driver notices, and approves — and that is not comfort. You commit to stay calm. It carries you into Castle while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

You bolt three steps into snow past your knees, and the wolves stop howling to listen. You climb back in by yourself. You commit to run. It carries you into Castle while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

nodes.text: The doors are twice your height and open with no hand on them. No footman takes your bag. No fire is lit, yet the hall is warm, and supper waits under a cloth, still steaming, laid for exactly one. Your host appears at the top of the stair — courteous, white-haired, delighted — and says your name as though he has been practising it for months.

choices.consequence: You bow, and praise the hall, and he beams for an hour. Only later do you notice he never once ate. You be polite. The way toward Mirror Shave opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

You count the doors while he talks. Every one is locked. He watches you count, and says nothing at all. You look for an exit. The way toward Mirror Shave opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: You are shaving by the window when he wishes you good morning from directly over your shoulder — and the glass shows only an empty room. Your hand jumps. The razor opens a thin red line beneath your jaw. For one second his face becomes something with no courtesy in it whatsoever. Then he takes the mirror and hurls it into the courtyard.

choices.consequence: You write it up that night in careful shorthand he cannot read. Setting it down does not make it any smaller. You commit to note it. It carries you into Three Sisters while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

You decide it was the light, the fatigue, the poor Continental glass. You decide this several times before dawn. You choose to don't note. By Three Sisters, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

nodes.text: You fall asleep in the one room he told you never to sleep in. Three women step out of the moonlight — two dark, one fair — arguing pleasantly over who gets first turn at you. The fair one kneels. You feel her breath, then her teeth just touching, and you are ashamed of how much of you wants her to go on. Then the door bursts inward.

choices.consequence: The prayer comes out in your mother's voice, which surprises you. It does not save you. He does, and that is worse. You pray. The way toward Letters opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.
Your legs will not obey. You learn something about yourself in that second you will never write in the journal. You run. The way toward Letters opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: He asks you, so very kindly, to write three letters home and date them weeks apart. The last one says you have already left the castle safely. You understand precisely what that is: a timetable for how long you have left. Downstairs, Mina's letter waits on the salver — cheerful, ordinary, full of train times and a wedding date — and you cannot make yourself open it.

choices.consequence: You write nothing true and everything comforting. Somewhere in England a woman reads it and sleeps well, and that must be enough. You reply carefully. The way toward Whitby opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

The letter stays folded in your breast pocket, going soft at the creases. Silence is its own kind of message. You commit to don't reply. It carries you into Whitby while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

nodes.text: A schooner runs aground at Whitby in a storm with every sail set and not one living soul aboard. The captain is lashed to his own wheel, dead, a crucifix wound through his fingers. An enormous dog leaps from the bow before anyone can reach her and goes up the abbey steps and is never seen again. The cargo: fifty crates of earth, consigned to a buyer who never appears.

choices.consequence: You cut the notice from the Gazette and keep it. Later it will be the first page of the file that saves you. You commit to mark it. It carries you into Lucy while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.
It is a storm story. This coast has one every winter. You turn the page, and the tide comes in anyway. You don't mark. The way toward Lucy opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: Lucy begins walking in her sleep — out through the door, up the East Cliff in her nightdress, barefoot on wet stone. Each morning she is paler and sweeter and less able to explain any of it. At her throat, two small punctures, precise as a bookbinder's awl, that close by afternoon and open again by dark. She asks you, laughing, please not to make a fuss.

choices.consequence: The Dutchman comes at once and asks not one question, which tells you he has seen this exact thing before. You choose to bring Van Helsing. By Garlic, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.
You give it a week to resolve itself. In a week there is nothing left of her to resolve. You wait. The way toward Garlic opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: Van Helsing hangs garlic flower at the sash, at the door, and in a wreath around her neck, and forbids anyone to move so much as a stem. Lucy sleeps deep and wakes rosy for the first time in a month. Then a well-meaning maid finds the room stinking, throws the windows wide to air it, and clears the whole lot away with the breakfast things.

choices.consequence: You lay it all again and stand the watch yourself, and do not sleep. It buys her three more days. You commit to repeat the cure. It carries you into Lucy Dies while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

You tell yourself the flowers were superstition dressed up as medicine. The shadows under her eyes go the colour of thunder. You commit to move on. It carries you into Lucy Dies while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

nodes.text: It takes four transfusions from four different men, and at the end of it she is not saved. In the last hour her voice drops into something low and hungry and she asks Arthur to kiss her — and Van Helsing hauls him back by the collar so hard they both go down. Then it passes. She is briefly, entirely Lucy again. Then she is nothing at all.

choices.consequence: You sit with the body until dawn because that is what one does for people. You do not yet know it is a mistake. You choose to mourn. By Lucy Undead, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.
You swear it in a room that smells of iron and lilies. Van Helsing says nothing, which is how he agrees. You vow. The way toward Lucy Undead opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: The Westminster papers name her the Bloofer Lady. Children go missing on the Heath after dark and come home by morning cheerful and weak, describing a beautiful lady who wanted to play, unable to account for the two small marks. Van Helsing takes you to the tomb at midnight and levers up the lid. She is warmer now than she ever was alive.

choices.consequence: It takes a stake, a hammer, and the man who loved her holding the point steady. Her face afterward is finally at peace. None of yours ever will be.

You cannot do it. She rises the next night, and a child is carried home the night after that. Mercy keeps a body count too. You don't. The way toward Mina opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: Mina takes every letter, journal, telegram and phonograph cylinder the five of you have been hoarding separately, and types them into one chronological record. Overnight the impossible becomes a case file. Laid out in order, the shape of the thing finally appears: patient, methodical, three centuries old, and currently buying property across London through respectable solicitors.

choices.consequence: You hand her everything. She is faster than all of you and twice as unsentimental about what it means. You commit to trust her. It carries you into Renfield while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

You agree, gently, to shield her from the worst of it. You will pay for that agreement with her blood. You choose to hide things from her. By Renfield, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

nodes.text: The lunatic in Seward's asylum eats flies, then spiders fattened on flies, then sparrows fattened on spiders — building life upward, he explains, one small ration at a time. He keeps a ledger. He is calm, precise and entirely lucid on every subject but one: the Master is coming, the Master is near, and Renfield has been very good and would like his reward now.

choices.consequence: You let him talk and you take notes, and he gives you the address before any of the rest of you work it out. You commit to listen. It carries you into The Boxes while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

You file him as a case study and close the door. He goes quiet, which ought to frighten you more than the shouting did. You choose to don't listen. By The Boxes, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

nodes.text: Fifty crates of Transylvanian earth, landed at Whitby, carted across London by three separate haulage firms. He cannot rest on English ground and cannot cross running water at will — so every box is a bed, and every bed is a fortress. Nine went to Carfax. The rest are scattered through Bermondsey, Mile End and Piccadilly. You are not hunting a man. You are besieging an address book.

choices.consequence: You spend a fortnight on carters' receipts and bills of lading. Dull, unglamorous, exhausting work — and the thing that wins. You track them. The way toward Mina Bitten opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

You go straight at him instead, and he is never where he is. He has fifty places to be. You have one. You commit to don't track. It carries you into Mina Bitten while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

nodes.text: You have been keeping her out of it for her own good, sleeping in the next room with the door shut. That is precisely where he finds her. When you break in he has Seward face-down on the floor and Mina held against his opened chest, being made to drink — and he turns and smiles at all five of you, entirely unhurried, before the mist takes him out through the sash.

choices.text: Bring her into the planning fully
choices.consequence: You tell her every single thing from that hour onward. The link runs both ways: he can find her, and through her, she can find him. You bring her into the planning fully. The way toward Wafer opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.
You move to spare her a second time. She is now the only one of you who knows where he is, and you have decided she should not be told anything.

nodes.text: Van Helsing touches the Host to her forehead to bless her, and it burns — a livid raised scar, red as a brand, and permanent. Mina puts her hand flat over it and says the word none of the rest of you will say aloud: unclean. Then she makes you promise, all of you, in writing, that if she turns you will do to her exactly what you did to Lucy.

choices.consequence: You promise her the scar will fade. You have not one shred of evidence for it, and you say it anyway. You commit to vow she will be cleansed. It carries you into Box Hunt while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

You look at her forehead and see the ending, and she watches you see it. It is the cruellest thing you do all year. You commit to despair. It carries you into Box Hunt while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

nodes.text: House to house with a locksmith's picks and Van Helsing's wafers, breaking the earth in every crate so he can never lie in it again. Carfax first, then Bermondsey, then Mile End. He is always one address ahead of you. In the Piccadilly hallway he walks straight past your shoulder, laughing, close enough to touch — and you cannot make your hand move.

choices.consequence: You sanctify forty-nine and check the manifest twice over. The fiftieth is already on a cart bound for the docks. You commit to be thorough. It carries you into Train Across Europe while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

Speed costs you two crates you never confirm. You will lie awake for years wondering which two they were. You choose to be fast. By Train Across Europe, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

nodes.text: He runs for home in the last box, by sea, aboard the Czarina Catherine. Mina, hypnotised at sunrise, reports lapping water and creaking timber and darkness — she is looking out through his eyes, and she does not enjoy it. So you split: one party overland by train through Paris and Bucharest, one up the river by launch, all of you racing a ship none of you can see.

choices.consequence: You wire ahead at every station and arrive as one body. Unheroic, procedural, and the only reason any of you survive it. You choose to coordinate. By Carpathian Pass, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

You go flat out and arrive first and alone, in deep snow, with nobody holding the far side of the pass. You commit to race. It carries you into Carpathian Pass while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

nodes.text: Snow to the axles and the light going fast off the ridge. A band of Szgany drive a wagon hard for the castle with the last box roped to the bed — armed, loyal, and fully aware of what they are carrying. Behind you Mina waits inside a ring of crumbled Host that the three sisters circle all night long, calling her by name in voices she recognises.

choices.consequence: You take the high road and come down on them at the bend. It works because they never see the second party at all. You choose to cut off the cart. By Sunset, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

You ride straight at forty men and trust to nerve. Two of you are cut before the wagon has even stopped. You choose to approach openly. By Sunset, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

nodes.text: The wagon goes over, the Szgany scatter into the trees, and the lid comes off with a crowbar. He lies in the earth with his eyes open and aware, waiting out the last inches of sun above the ridge — minutes, then seconds. Harker's kukri and Morris's bowie go in together, throat and heart, and for one instant the whole ancient thing looks almost grateful.

choices.consequence: Harker's blade takes the neck clean through. It has to be both, at the same moment, or neither one counts. You commit to strike at the throat. It carries you into Mina's Forehead while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

Morris drives the bowie home with a hole already opened in his own side, and does not let go until it is done. You choose to strike at the heart. By Mina's Forehead, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

nodes.text: He goes to dust in the space of one breath — no scream, no curse, no vengeance, only the long-postponed peace of it. And Mina, standing in the snow with the light coming back into the sky, puts her fingers to her forehead and finds nothing there at all. The scar is gone as though it had never burned. Quincey Morris sees it, says so, and dies about a minute later, smiling.

choices.consequence: You reach her before your legs give out, and neither of you says anything for a very long time. You hold her. The way toward Years Later opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

You say the words over Morris in the snow, badly, and everyone joins in badly, and it is the best funeral he could have wanted. You pray. The way toward Years Later opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: Seven years on there is a boy who carries the name of every man who stood in that pass, and he is loud, and ordinary, and appallingly healthy. This summer you take him east. The castle is a broken tooth on the ridge; the villagers still cross themselves at the name. At home, in a trunk, sits a bundle of typed pages with your own handwriting crowded into the margins.

choices.consequence: You give him the papers on his eighteenth birthday and let him decide for himself what to believe. You choose to tell him the truth. By The Record, the danger will know a little more about you than you know about it.

You let him have a childhood without it. Some inheritances are a kindness to withhold. You commit to don't tell him. It carries you into Quiet Years while the safer possibility closes without making a sound.

There is a version of this where you go back alone, and it has been waiting patiently for you to choose it. You take the third path. The way toward The Castle, Empty opens, and something on the other side seems to notice.

nodes.text: Mina binds it all together — shorthand journals, phonograph transcripts, the ship's log, the telegrams — and writes a note at the front admitting there is not one shred of proof in the entire volume. Not a single original document survives. The book outlives every one of you, and every reader who opens it runs the same arithmetic and arrives at the same place: it cannot possibly be true, and yet.

You marry. You have a son. You take a house with good light and you never once go back. The nightmares thin out over a decade and then mostly stop, and you grow old in England with dirt under your fingernails from a garden you genuinely love. The castle becomes a ruin, then a rumour, then one line in a guidebook. You outlive it, which is the whole of the victory.

Years later you go back alone, without telling anyone, and the villagers make the old sign as you pass. You climb to the great hall and sit down in the dust and the birdsong and wait for something to want something from you. Nothing does. That, in the end, is what you came for — to sit in the worst room of your life and find it empty, and stand up, and leave again.
